title: Copying the option with stock and cash
objectives: Price an option by building a portfolio with the same payoff.
Use the law of one price to find an arbitrage when an option is mispriced.

screens.title: What the call pays
screens.prose: A call struck at £100 gives you the right to buy the share for £100 in a year. The share ends at £120 or £80.

state.caption: The share today and in a year

screens.question: Fill in the call’s payoff in each state.

hints.text: Would you pay £100 for the share in each state?
At £120 you buy for £100 a share worth £120.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The call pays $\max(S_1 - 100, 0)$ in each state.

byKey.r0c1: At £120 you buy for £100 a share worth £120: $\max(120 - 100, 0) = 20$.
byKey.r1c1: At £80 nobody pays £100 for the share, so the call pays $\max(80 - 100, 0) = 0$, not a negative amount.

explain.text: The call pays £20 if up and nothing if down. What is that worth today? We will build it from things we can already price: shares and cash.

screens.title: Shares and cash
screens.prose: Hold $\Delta$ shares and some cash, received in a year if positive and owed if negative. In a year the holding is worth $\Delta S_1$ plus the cash: a straight line in the share price $S_1$.

derive.caption: Up: holding £{{fixed(120*D + L, 2)}}, call £20.00. Down: holding £{{fixed(80*D + L, 2)}}, call £0.00.

screens.question: Make the line pass through both call payoffs. How many shares $\Delta$ does that take?

widget.label: Number of shares
widget.accept: 0.5 shares, with £40 owed in a year.

hints.text: Between £80 and £120 the call gains £20. How many shares gain £20 over that range?
The slope of the line is $\Delta$. It must climb £20 over £40.

feedback.correct: Half a share, with £40 owed in a year, matches both points.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Get both dashed gaps to zero, then read off the shares.

byKey.one: One share gains £40 between the states, twice what the call gains. The line is too steep.
byKey.none: With no shares the line is flat, but the call pays more when the share is higher.

explain.text: Half a share gains £20 between the two states, exactly what the call gains. Owing £40 then sets the level: $0.5 \times 80 - 40 = 0$ and $0.5 \times 120 - 40 = 20$. The line meets the kinked payoff at both prices the tree allows.

screens.title: Cash today
screens.prose: Your holding is $\Delta = 0.5$ shares and £40 owed in a year. You borrow today at 5%, and the debt grows by 5% over the year.

derive.caption: Up: holding £{{fixed(120*D + L, 2)}}, call £20.00. Down: holding £{{fixed(80*D + L, 2)}}, call £0.00.

screens.question: How much do you borrow today?

hints.text: If you borrow $B$ today, how much do you owe in a year?
You owe $1.05$ times what you borrow, and the line’s cash is the £40 owed.
$1.05 \times \text{borrowed} = 40$, so divide 40 by 1.05.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the amount that grows to £40 at 5%.

byKey.no-discount: That is what you owe in a year. Borrowing it today would leave you owing £42.
byKey.add-interest: You added interest to £40. The £40 is the debt in a year, so take the interest out: $40/1.05$.
byKey.subtract: You took 5% off £40. But $38 \times 1.05 = 39.90$, so divide by 1.05 instead.

explain.text: Borrowing £38.10 today means owing $40$ in a year. So the copy is 0.5 shares and a loan of £38.10: a **replicating portfolio**. We write $B = -38.10$, cash today, negative when borrowed.

screens.title: The copy, state by state
screens.prose: The copy holds 0.5 shares and borrows £38.10 at 5%. Fill in the loan and the copy in a year, then what the copy costs today.

state.caption: The copy: 0.5 shares and £40 owed in a year

screens.question: Complete the table.

hints.text: Owing is negative. How much do you owe in a year?
The loan grows by 5%: $38.10 \times 1.05$.
Loan: $-40$ in both states. Copy: add each column, so today $50 - 38.10$.

feedback.correct: The copy pays £20 or £0 and costs £11.90 today.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Owing is negative, and each copy cell is the sum of the column above it.

byKey.r1c2: The loan grows by 5%: you owe $38.10 \times 1.05 = 40$, written $-40$.
byKey.r1c3: You owe the same £40 in the down state. The loan does not care how the share did.
byKey.r2c1: The copy costs the shares less what you borrowed: $50 - 38.10$.

explain.text: The copy pays £20 up and £0 down, exactly like the call. It costs $50 - 38.10 = \text{£}11.90$ today. So the call must cost £11.90 too.

canvas.caption: Copy and call both pay £20 or £0; the copy costs £11.90

screens.title: A call at £14
screens.prose: Suppose the call trades at £14 in the market. You can still build its copy for £11.90.

state.caption: Sell the dear one, buy the cheap one

screens.question: How much do you keep today?

hints.text: Selling brings cash in; buying sends it out.
The net row adds the column above it.

feedback.correct: You keep £2.10 now and owe nothing net later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two cash flows today.

byKey.sale-only: You counted only the sale. Buying the copy costs £11.90.
byKey.sign: You receive £14 and pay £11.90, so you keep money.
byKey.added: You added the copy’s cost. Buying it sends £11.90 out.

explain.text: You keep £2.10 today, and the two trades cancel in both states. Two things with the same payoff in every state must have the same price: the **law of one price**. At any other price the gap is an arbitrage.

screens.title: Copying a put
screens.prose: A put struck at £100 pays £0 if the share ends at £120 and £20 if it ends at £80. Copy it with $\Delta$ shares and cash $B$ today, at 5%.

state.caption: The put pays when the share falls

screens.question: Find the copy and the put’s price.

hints.text: The put loses £20 as the share rises by £40. Which way must the shares face?
A short position loses when the share rises: $\Delta$ is negative.

feedback.correct: Short half a share and lend £57.14: the put costs £7.14.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the put in both states, then price the copy.

byKey.r0c1: The put falls by £20 as the share rises by £40. That needs a short position: $\Delta = -0.5$, not $+0.5$.
byKey.r1c1: Use the up state: $120\Delta + 1.05B = 0$ with $\Delta = -0.5$. Cash is positive here: you lend.

explain.text: Short half a share and lend £57.14: up, $-60 + 60 = 0$; down, $-40 + 60 = 20$. The put costs $-50 + 57.14 = \text{£}7.14$. A put is copied by selling shares and lending, the mirror of the call.

screens.title: Using the odds
screens.prose: Analysts give the share a 0.8 chance of rising. A colleague prices the call at its expected payoff, discounted: $0.8 \times 20 / 1.05 = \text{£}15.24$.
screens.question: What should the call cost?

options.why: You weighted the payoffs by the real chances. At £15.24 you could sell the call and buy the £11.90 copy, keeping £3.33 riskless.
You took the expected payoff and did not discount it. And the real chance does not price the call anyway: the copy does.
You borrowed £40, the amount owed in a year. Today you can borrow only $40/1.05 = \text{£}38.10$, so the copy costs £11.90.

hints.text: What does the copy cost, and does it depend on the 0.8?
The copy pays £20 or £0 whichever state happens.
The copy costs £11.90 whatever the chances, so the call must too.

feedback.correct: £11.90, the cost of the copy, whatever the chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the call by its copy, not by a forecast.

byKey.ev: You weighted the payoffs by the real chances. At £15.24 you could sell the call and buy the £11.90 copy, keeping £3.33 riskless.
byKey.no-interest: You borrowed £40, the amount owed in a year. Today you can borrow only $40/1.05 = \text{£}38.10$.

explain.text: The copy pays the call’s payoff in both states, whatever the chances. So the call costs what the copy costs, £11.90. The 0.8 never entered your working.

screens.title: Two equations
screens.prose: Write the copy’s two conditions, one per state, and solve them as in the vectors course. Here $B$ is cash today, so it is worth $1.05B$ in a year.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $120\Delta + 1.05B = 20$ and $80\Delta + 1.05B = 0$: the copy pays what the call pays in each state
$40\Delta = 20$: subtract the second equation from the first, so the cash cancels
$1.05B = -40$, so $B = -38.10$: put $\Delta = 0.5$ into the down equation, then divide by 1.05
$c_0 = 100\Delta + B = 50 - 38.10 = 11.90$: the copy’s cost today is the call’s price

hints.text: Start from the two conditions, one per state.
Subtracting the equations removes $B$ first.
Conditions, subtract, divide, substitute, then price.

feedback.correct: Subtract to find $\Delta$, substitute to find $B$, then price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the one before it.

byKey.e4: $B$ needs $\Delta$ first, so it comes after $\Delta = 0.5$.
byKey.e5: The price needs both $\Delta$ and $B$, so it comes last.

explain.text: Subtracting removes the cash, since it pays the same in both states. That leaves the shares to match the call’s £20 gain over the share’s £40. Then either equation gives $B$.

screens.title: Any one-step option
screens.prose: You solved the same two equations each time. For any one-step tree, $$\Delta = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}, \quad B = \frac{c_d - \Delta S_d}{1 + r}, \quad c_0 = \Delta S_0 + B.$$
screens.question: Which number never appeared in your working?

options.text: The chance the share goes up

options.why: You used it to discount the loan: $B = -40/1.05$.

options.text: The two share prices in a year
options.why: They set $\Delta$: the call’s gain over the share’s gain, $20/40$.
The strike fixed the call’s payoffs, £20 and £0.

hints.text: Look back at the two equations. What went into them?
Prices, payoffs and the rate went in. Nothing about how likely each state is.

feedback.correct: No chance of up appears anywhere.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List what the two equations used.

explain.text: The copy uses the two prices, the payoffs and the rate. It never asks how likely each state is. That is why every trader, whatever their forecast, must agree on £11.90.

screens.title: A bank prices a call
screens.prose: A bank sells a client a one-year call on a share at £250, struck at £260. The share ends at £300 or £200. The bank borrows at 4% and prices the call by its copy.

state.caption: The bank’s one-step model of the share

screens.question: Find the copy per call and the price.

hints.text: The call gains £40 while the share gains £100.
$\Delta = 40/100$. In the down state the shares are worth $0.4 \times 200 = 80$.
Borrow $80/1.04$. The price is $0.4 \times 250$ minus that.

feedback.correct: 0.4 shares and £76.92 borrowed: the call is worth £23.08.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the call in both states, discounting at 4%.

byKey.r0c1: The call gains $40 - 0$ while the share gains $300 - 200$. Divide the first by the second.
byKey.r1c1: In the down state the loan must cancel $0.4 \times 200 = 80$. Borrow $80/1.04$ today.

explain.text: $\Delta = 40/100 = 0.4$, and the bank borrows $80/1.04 = \text{£}76.92$ per call. The copy costs $100 - 76.92 = \text{£}23.08$. Charging less would cost the bank money on its hedge.

ideas: Hold $\Delta$ shares and cash $B$ so that the holding pays what the option pays in both states.
Solve two equations: $\Delta = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}$, then $B$ from either state, discounting at $1 + r$.
The option costs what its copy costs: the law of one price. The real chance of up never enters.

formula.name: Replication price
formula.tex: c_0 = \Delta S_0 + B, \quad \Delta = \dfrac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}, \quad B = \dfrac{c_d - \Delta S_d}{1 + r}
formula.note: $B < 0$ means borrowing. A put has $\Delta < 0$ and $B > 0$: short shares and lend.

summary.trap: Pricing by the expected payoff with real chances gives the wrong price; so does forgetting the interest on the loan.

quiz.prose: A share at £50 ends at £60 or £40 in a year, and the rate is 5%. A call struck at £50 pays £10 or £0.
quiz.question: What does the call cost today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\Delta$ and the loan, then price the copy.

byKey.no-interest: You borrowed £20, the amount owed in a year. Borrow $20/1.05$ today.
byKey.half: You weighted the payoffs 50/50 and discounted. The copy, not a guess at the chances, sets the price.
byKey.payoff: That is the most the call can pay, in a year. Price the copy today.

explain.text: $\Delta = 10/20 = 0.5$. In the down state $0.5 \times 40 = 20$, so borrow $20/1.05 = \text{£}19.05$. The copy costs $25 - 19.05 = \text{£}5.95$.

quiz.prose: On the £100 tree the call’s copy costs £11.90. The call trades at £13.
quiz.question: Which trade locks in a riskless profit?

options.text: Sell the call and buy the copy
Buy the call and sell the copy
options.why: That pays £11.90 for the copy’s mirror and £13 for the call: you lose £1.10.

options.text: Buy the call and hold it
options.why: That is a bet on the share rising. If it falls, the call pays nothing.

options.text: Sell the call and hold nothing
options.why: If the share rises you owe £20 with nothing to pay it from.

feedback.correct: Sell the dear call, buy the cheap copy: £1.10 now.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sell what is too dear and buy its copy.

explain.text: You receive £13 and pay £11.90, keeping £1.10. In a year the copy pays exactly what you owe on the call, in both states.

quiz.prose: Same tree: £50 today, £60 or £40 in a year, rate 5%. A put struck at £50 pays £0 or £10.
quiz.question: Which holding copies the put?

options.why: That is the call’s copy. The put pays when the share falls, so you need to be short.
Check the up state: $-60 + 52.50 = -7.50$, not 0. One share is twice too many.
£30 is what you need in a year. Lend $30/1.05 = \text{£}28.57$ today.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each holding in both states.

explain.text: $\Delta = (0 - 10)/20 = -0.5$. In the up state the short costs $30$, so lend $30/1.05 = \text{£}28.57$. The put costs $-25 + 28.57 = \text{£}3.57$.
